source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), complete user-provided Chapter 3 Part B (Harrell, Segal discussion, Schmitz); Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199

coverage.scope: B. Inclusions: Harrell revocable expectations, Segal contingent interests, Schmitz postpetition federal fishing quotas

topics.title: B. In re Harrell — Season Tickets and Revocable Renewal Expectations
topics.description: Ninth Circuit; Phoenix Suns renewal privileges under Arizona law and conflict with broad federal property concept.

entries.title: In re Harrell, 73 F.3d 218 (9th Cir. 1996)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), complete user-provided Chapter 3 Part B (Harrell, Segal discussion, Schmitz); Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: No. Under Arizona law, unguaranteed chance of renewal is merely a speculative expectancy, not a legally enforceable property right; Ninth Circuit affirmed district court's exclusion of renewal opportunity.
entries.laymanExplanation: Where creditor/debtor has only unprotected revocable renewal expectancy and other party retains absolute discretion, state law may leave no debtor property right for §541(a)(1) estate.
entries.legalExplanation: Ninth Circuit applied Butner and Arizona decisions Gannett/Whiteco, emphasizing holders cannot compel Suns to renew even if nearly always offered. Transferable tickets for existing season differ from right to renew new contract; possible market price for chance doesn't create enforceable entitlement. Court distinguished Pennsylvania precedent permitting Steelers season-ticket renewal sale.
entries.examApplication: Compare current season tickets versus next year's privilege, Suns terms, applicable AZ law, Pennsylvania NFL case distinction.
entries.examTrap: Do not claim existing fully paid ticket or currently granted playoff ticket was categorically excluded; decision specifically concerns renewal opportunity.
entries.sourceRole: Full judicial opinion excerpt in the uploaded Chapter 3
entries.facts: Trustee sought to sell debtor's Phoenix Suns season and playoff tickets and opportunity to renew future season tickets. Suns notices each year described renewal as a revocable privilege and denied any guarantee; team's discretionary renewal power remained. Bankruptcy judge allowed sale; district court rejected renewal privilege as state-law property and trustee appealed.
entries.issue: Is a highly probable but contractually revocable opportunity to renew future Phoenix Suns season tickets property of the estate under §541(a)(1)?
entries.holding: No. Under Arizona law, unguaranteed chance of renewal is merely a speculative expectancy, not a legally enforceable property right; Ninth Circuit affirmed district court's exclusion of renewal opportunity.
entries.reasoning: Ninth Circuit applied Butner and Arizona decisions Gannett/Whiteco, emphasizing holders cannot compel Suns to renew even if nearly always offered. Transferable tickets for existing season differ from right to renew new contract; possible market price for chance doesn't create enforceable entitlement. Court distinguished Pennsylvania precedent permitting Steelers season-ticket renewal sale.
entries.rule: Where creditor/debtor has only unprotected revocable renewal expectancy and other party retains absolute discretion, state law may leave no debtor property right for §541(a)(1) estate.

entries.title: Arizona Gannett rule: expectation is not legal entitlement
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), complete user-provided Chapter 3 Part B (Harrell, Segal discussion, Schmitz); Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Even longstanding practice of renewing leases or tickets doesn't transform a landlord/team's uncommitted intention into presently enforceable renewal interest.
entries.laymanExplanation: 'They always renew me' is not the same as 'they must renew me.'
entries.legalExplanation: If counterparty can decline each year, renewal's value may be speculative rather than legal property under applicable nonbankruptcy law.
entries.examApplication: Ask what written agreement promises and whether holder can compel renewal.
entries.examTrap: Economic probability and legal enforceability separate.

entries.title: Why Harrell and Chicago Board of Trade are in tension
entries.page: Ch. 3 § B / Harrell and Johnson (syllabus pp.171–199)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), complete user-provided Chapter 3 Part B (Harrell, Segal discussion, Schmitz); Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Johnson looked past Illinois nonproperty label to find transferable economic seat, but Harrell relied heavily on Arizona's denial of enforceable right; court treats expectations differently from existing legally transferable membership.
entries.laymanExplanation: A seat that can be sold under conditions is not the same as an offer for seats that nobody must make.
entries.legalExplanation: Analytical reconciliation: state law sets whether enforceable underlying interest exists; federal definition decides inclusion, not state label. Casebook deliberately asks whether Harrell is faithful to Johnson.
entries.examApplication: In compare-and-contrast essay argue both why Harrell fits Butner and why Johnson could imply broader property test.
entries.examTrap: Neither case says market value alone is conclusive in every circumstance.

entries.title: §541(c)(1)(A) discussion: restrictions on transfer
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), complete user-provided Chapter 3 Part B (Harrell, Segal discussion, Schmitz); Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: The book asks whether anti-transfer clauses might be overridden by §541(c)(1)(A), in contrast to situation where debtor had no underlying enforceable right at all.
entries.laymanExplanation: Clause restricting transfer of an existing contract is different from lack of contract to renew at all.
entries.legalExplanation: §541(c)(1) generally brings interests into estate despite provisions restricting transfer, but does not fabricate a nonexistent substantive right.
entries.examApplication: If there is some renewal right subject only to no-assignment term, compare §541(c)(1) with pure revocable discretion.
entries.examTrap: Don't automatically equate nonassignable interest to nonproperty.

entries.title: If trustee sold 'renewal opportunity,' what could purchaser enforce?
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), complete user-provided Chapter 3 Part B (Harrell, Segal discussion, Schmitz); Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Question remains what legal rights a buyer would receive if Suns can refuse renewal; Harrell majority says none against Suns.
entries.laymanExplanation: Paying for a chance does not give buyer a guaranteed seat next year.
entries.legalExplanation: This is casebook's policy/analytical question left for self-testing; no assigned problem answered.
entries.examApplication: Analyze enforceability rather than just sale price.
entries.examTrap: Avoid adding guaranteed contractual right to buyer without support.

topics.title: B. Segal v. Rochelle — The ‘Sufficiently Rooted’ Contingent-Interest Principle
topics.description: Referenced Supreme Court case summarized by casebook, not a full brief; tax refund roots and postpetition conditions.

entries.title: Segal v Rochelle (1966) — prepetition losses and later tax refunds
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), complete user-provided Chapter 3 Part B (Harrell, Segal discussion, Schmitz); Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Debtors' federal income-tax loss-carryback refunds could not be claimed until tax year closed after filing, but filing-date prepetition tax payments and operative business losses were already present; Supreme Court treated claims as estate property.
entries.laymanExplanation: A refund check arrives later, but the meaningful tax payments and losses creating it had already occurred.
entries.legalExplanation: Casebook describes Supreme Court 'sufficiently rooted in prebankruptcy past' analysis, emphasizing present contingent interest despite later formal vesting.
entries.examApplication: For asset received after filing separate substantive origin from date cash/check delivered.
entries.examTrap: Segal discussion is NOT a full opinion excerpt in Chapter 3.

entries.title: ‘Rooted in prebankruptcy past’ is about substantive prepetition events
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), complete user-provided Chapter 3 Part B (Harrell, Segal discussion, Schmitz); Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Uncertain future amount/date does not necessarily bar estate inclusion where all legally significant qualifying facts had occurred by petition, despite remaining formal conditions.
entries.laymanExplanation: All ingredients for refund are already in the bowl, even if IRS must wait for tax year to end.
entries.legalExplanation: Segal looks at tax law creation and content of refund interest, not just name on future check.
entries.examApplication: Draw timeline prepetition tax payments, losses, end of tax year, refund application and payment.
entries.examTrap: Don't collapse 'later receipt' into 'later created right'.

entries.title: Segal and Schmitz: competing ways to view contingency
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), complete user-provided Chapter 3 Part B (Harrell, Segal discussion, Schmitz); Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Segal's past losses had already set legal conditions for refund under existing law; Schmitz's future fishing allotment did not exist under any adopted regulation at filing.
entries.laymanExplanation: Existing lottery ticket with contingent prize differs from government creating a lottery after bankruptcy.
entries.legalExplanation: In Schmitz future legal enactment and discretionary award created right, not merely matured preexisting claim.
entries.examApplication: For contingent licenses ask whether law existed and debtor had legally cognizable application right at petition.
entries.examTrap: Having past work history that eventually affects award is not by itself debtor's estate property.

topics.title: B. In re Schmitz — Fishing Rights Created After Petition
topics.description: Ninth Circuit full opinion on postpetition quota regulations and prefiling work history, contrast with Segal.

entries.title: In re Schmitz, 270 F.3d 1254 (9th Cir. 2001)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), complete user-provided Chapter 3 Part B (Harrell, Segal discussion, Schmitz); Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: No. No quota regulations or rights legally existed at filing; prepetition catch history was only expectancy that lawmakers might later create opportunities. Future rights govern postpetition fishing activity, not compensation for past work. Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded.
entries.laymanExplanation: Property under §541(a)(1) must be debtor's actual existing interest at commencement, not hoped-for interest dependent on postpetition new law; future rights reflecting work history not necessarily estate proceeds.
entries.legalExplanation: Federal fishery regulations defined rights; proposed rulemaking uncertain until finalized. Even if quota allocations referenced 1988–90 past catches, like current salary influenced by old education, connection doesn't make entire new earning opportunity prepetition property. Contingent-right cases had preexisting binding statutes/contracts; here legal creation itself postpetition. Fresh-start rationale supported debtor retaining rights.
entries.examApplication: Timeline: 1992 filing, Nov1993 rule, 1994 effective/application, Dec1996 certificates, 1997 sales. Test existence of qualifying law, required steps and nature as compensation vs prospect.
entries.examTrap: Holding is not that all postpetition receipts linked to prepetition services escape estate (compare Segal and Andrews).
entries.sourceRole: Full judicial opinion excerpt in the uploaded Chapter 3
entries.facts: Commercial Alaska fisherman caught halibut/sablefish 1988–90, filed Chapter 7 April 7, 1992 while proposed fisheries quota program merely under study. Commerce adopted final regulations Nov.1993 effective Jan.1994; Schmitz applied 1994 and got quota certificates Dec.1996; he sold allocations Jan.1997 for ~$44,360.50 and $2,205. Trustee sued to recover proceeds and revoke discharge; bankruptcy court/BAP treated quotas as rooted in prefiling catch history.
entries.issue: Were the federally created quota-share/individual-fishing-quota rights issued years after bankruptcy included in estate under §541(a)(1) because calculated from debtor's prepetition fishing history?
entries.holding: No. No quota regulations or rights legally existed at filing; prepetition catch history was only expectancy that lawmakers might later create opportunities. Future rights govern postpetition fishing activity, not compensation for past work. Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded.
entries.reasoning: Federal fishery regulations defined rights; proposed rulemaking uncertain until finalized. Even if quota allocations referenced 1988–90 past catches, like current salary influenced by old education, connection doesn't make entire new earning opportunity prepetition property. Contingent-right cases had preexisting binding statutes/contracts; here legal creation itself postpetition. Fresh-start rationale supported debtor retaining rights.
entries.rule: Property under §541(a)(1) must be debtor's actual existing interest at commencement, not hoped-for interest dependent on postpetition new law; future rights reflecting work history not necessarily estate proceeds.

entries.title: The timing rule — regulations not adopted at filing
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), complete user-provided Chapter 3 Part B (Harrell, Segal discussion, Schmitz); Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: An agency consideration or proposed rule is not a legal entitlement to benefit under a program that might not exist in that form; court noted comment and objections can prevent finalization.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can't own a fishing quota before government creates fishing quota rights.
entries.legalExplanation: At filing no final recommendation, notice of proposed rule or assurance program would be implemented as favorable to debtor.
entries.examApplication: For tax credit or subsidy not yet enacted, ask whether legislature created right before filing.
entries.examTrap: Agency discussing a plan for years ≠ vested entitlement.

entries.title: Catch history serves future earning capacity rather than deferred compensation
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), complete user-provided Chapter 3 Part B (Harrell, Segal discussion, Schmitz); Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Quota governed future fishing catches; past landing records used as metric for who may harvest, not an unpaid fee for historical fish already sold.
entries.laymanExplanation: Old resume gets you future job, but resume itself isn't owed salary from future employer.
entries.legalExplanation: Compare accrued commission/contingent contract payment earned before filing to privileges created later for future labor.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish property rights in prepetition goodwill from personal postpetition earning power.
entries.examTrap: Do not equate transferable quota's eventual economic value with property status 1992.

entries.title: Distinguishing binding contingency contracts
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), complete user-provided Chapter 3 Part B (Harrell, Segal discussion, Schmitz); Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Schmitz contrasted Neuton, Ryerson, Jess, Minoco and Bialac where prefiling enforceable trusts/contracts/contingent clauses existed and later conditions triggered payment.
entries.laymanExplanation: An existing contract that will pay if event occurs is more than hope an agency writes new rules.
entries.legalExplanation: Estate can hold a contingent claim subject to later future event; prepetition source of legal obligation decisive.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether necessary predicate was legal instrument in force, or government action creating brand-new legal asset.
entries.examTrap: A contingent right need not be liquid or currently payable to be estate property.

entries.title: In re Vote disaster payments analogy
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), complete user-provided Chapter 3 Part B (Harrell, Segal discussion, Schmitz); Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: The casebook opinion cited farmer whose prefiling crop loss preceded later Congressional crop-aid statute; subsequent disaster payment wasn't estate property because relief law created after petition.
entries.laymanExplanation: A crop loss last year doesn't mean farmer owned future disaster subsidy before Congress voted for one.
entries.legalExplanation: Statutory benefit must have legal basis at petition to qualify as presently existing contingent right under cited reasoning.
entries.examApplication: Use for after-enacted federal aid or relief checks.
entries.examTrap: Don't claim every postpetition tax refund resembles later disaster law; compare Segal.

entries.title: Fresh start and ex-ante versus ex-post valuation
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), complete user-provided Chapter 3 Part B (Harrell, Segal discussion, Schmitz); Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Debtor's post-bankruptcy income potential should be preserved; book asks whether eventual sales show 1992 catch history had market value and whether analysis should view 1992 uncertainties rather than later hindsight.
entries.laymanExplanation: Looking backward after $44k sale makes quota seem certain, but filing-date law was still uncertain.
entries.legalExplanation: Schmitz judges legal existence on filing date, not wealth eventually earned; valuation and legal status of prepetition rights are separate.
entries.examApplication: Discuss both ex ante likelihood and ex post realized value when contrasting Segal.
entries.examTrap: A property right's future sale price can't retroactively create the right at filing.

entries.title: Source's dissent? None excerpted; opinion reversed
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), complete user-provided Chapter 3 Part B (Harrell, Segal discussion, Schmitz); Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Excerpt contains Ninth Circuit majority opinion, not a separate dissent; appellate reversal of BAP also undercut prior discharge revocation.
entries.laymanExplanation: Trustee lost claim that the quota had been estate asset, so earlier basis to revoke discharge was remanded.
entries.legalExplanation: The source identifies bankruptcy court/BAP adverse holdings and Ninth Circuit final disposition.
entries.examApplication: Keep procedural posture clear in brief.
entries.examTrap: Do not fabricate dissent or characterize lower court analysis as Ninth Circuit holding.
